Summary adjusted using the Financial Stability Report (FSR):
- Policy stance: The FOMC keeps the federal funds rate at 0–0.25% and adopts outcome-based forward guidance under average inflation targeting, reflecting slack and below-target inflation. It will continue increasing Treasury and agency MBS holdings, and stands ready to use repo/ON RRP to support market functioning.
- FSR crosswalk: The FSR documents March 2020 dysfunction in the Treasury and short-term dollar funding markets and disrupted securitization; the Fed’s balance-sheet tools and facilities (e.g., SMCCF, CPFF, TALF, MLF, swap lines, FIMA repo) helped restore credit intermediation and ease funding pressures. This aligns with the statement’s emphasis on sustained asset purchases and operational tools to keep markets smooth and credit flowing.
- Risks and vulnerabilities: Despite improved financial conditions, the FSR highlights elevated vulnerabilities from COVID-19—high business leverage and speculative-grade credit risk, CRE valuation pressures, stress on nonbank mortgage servicers, rising delinquencies/default risks, and acute sectoral hits (energy, airlines, leisure). It also notes weaker household/SME balance sheets and reduced investor risk appetite, with global spillovers (Europe, China, EMEs). These reinforce the FOMC’s caution that the outlook depends on the virus and that risks remain considerable.
- Net read: The commitment to AIT and continued purchases is supportive for expectations and credit, but the FSR’s evidence of still-elevated financial vulnerabilities and prospective credit losses tilts the balance more negative than a policy-only reading.

Bottom line: Moderately negative tone given persistent systemic vulnerabilities and pandemic-related downside risks, partially offset by credible and comprehensive Fed support.
